introduction-the-orchestra-conductor.core: systemd is PID 1 and the system and service manager on most Linux distros. It starts units in parallel by dependency graph, supervises services (restarts and watchdogs), manages cgroups for resource control, collects logs (journald), handles timers (cron replacement), mounts, sockets, devices and user sessions, and provides uniform tooling (systemctl, journalctl, systemd-analyze). Understanding units and dependencies replaces a pile of init scripts.

first_principles.problem: A team manages services with ad-hoc shell scripts and nohup, and processes silently die without restart.

analogy.title: An orchestra conductor
analogy.story: Cues each section at the right time, notices when someone stops playing, and brings them back in.
analogy.breaks: Conductors improvise; systemd follows unit files.

code.text:
systemctl status nginx
systemctl enable --now nginx
systemctl restart nginx
journalctl -u nginx -f
systemctl list-units --type=service --state=failed

check.q: Name three things systemd manages besides starting services.
check.a: Logging (journald), timers, mounts, sockets, cgroup resource limits and user sessions (any three).

unit-files-the-instructions-systemd-read.core: A unit file has sections. [Unit] holds description, documentation and dependencies; the type-specific section ([Service]) holds Type= (simple, exec, forking, oneshot, notify), ExecStart=, User=, Restart=, Environment and EnvironmentFile, working directory, limits and sandboxing; [Install] holds WantedBy= for enablement. Vendor units live in /usr/lib/systemd/system and admin units in /etc/systemd/system. Run daemon-reload after edits and use systemd-analyze verify to lint.

first_principles.problem: A custom service unit starts, but systemd reports it 'active (exited)' while the process keeps running untracked.
truths: systemd must know how the process behaves.

analogy.title: A job description for a worker
analogy.story: It states who they are, when they start, how to tell they're working, and what to do if they stop.
analogy.breaks: Workers read descriptions once; systemd re-reads on daemon-reload.

code.text:
[Unit]
Description=Orders API
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=exec
User=orders
ExecStart=/opt/orders/bin/server --config /etc/orders/config.yaml
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=2
LimitNOFILE=65536
NoNewPrivileges=yes
ProtectSystem=strict
ReadWritePaths=/var/lib/orders

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

check.q: When should a service use Type=forking?
check.a: Only for traditional daemons that fork into the background and exit the parent; modern services should use simple/exec or notify.

types-of-units-services-timers-mounts-an.core: systemd manages many unit types. .service (processes), .socket (socket activation: systemd listens and starts the service on first connection), .timer (scheduled activation with calendar or monotonic triggers, persistent catch-up), .mount and .automount (filesystems, generated from fstab), .target (synchronisation points and groups), .path (activate on file changes), .slice (cgroup hierarchy), .scope (externally started processes) and .device (udev devices). Each is managed with the same systemctl verbs.

first_principles.problem: A nightly cron job silently fails, with no logs, retries or dependency on the network being up.
truths: Timers integrate with logging and dependencies.

analogy.title: Different kinds of staff rotas
analogy.story: Shift workers (services), on-call staff who start when the phone rings (sockets), and scheduled cleaners (timers).
analogy.breaks: Rotas are separate documents; systemd manages all with one tool.

example.title: Timer replacing cron

code.text:
# /etc/systemd/system/report.timer
[Timer]
OnCalendar=*-*-* 02:15:00
Persistent=true
RandomizedDelaySec=300
[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target

# /etc/systemd/system/report.service
[Unit]
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target
[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/opt/report/run.sh
# systemctl enable --now report.timer ; systemctl list-timers

example.outcome: right unit type for each job.

check.q: What does Persistent=true do in a systemd timer?
check.a: Runs a missed job at the next boot if the system was off at the scheduled time.

dependency-management-wants-requires-and.core: systemd separates requirement from ordering. Wants= is a weak dependency (start the other unit too, but don't fail if it fails), Requires= is strong (if it fails to start or stops, this unit stops too), BindsTo= is stronger still (tied to the other's active state), and PartOf= propagates stop and restart. Ordering is separate: After= and Before= only set sequence. Requires= without After= starts both in parallel, a common mistake.

first_principles.problem: An app with Requires=postgresql.service still starts before Postgres is ready and crashes.
truths: Needing a unit differs from ordering after it.

analogy.title: Inviting a friend vs waiting for them to arrive
analogy.story: Saying 'bring Alex' (Wants/Requires) doesn't mean waiting until Alex arrives (After).
analogy.breaks: Friends text when they arrive; services need notify/readiness to signal it.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: API starts only after Postgres is ready.

code.text:
[Unit]
Description=Orders API
Requires=postgresql.service
After=postgresql.service network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target
# Postgres unit uses Type=notify, so 'After' waits for real readiness

check.q: Does Requires= alone ensure a unit starts after its dependency?
check.a: No, Requires= only declares the dependency; you also need After= to enforce ordering.

targets-grouping-units-together.core: Targets are named synchronisation points that group units, much like the old runlevels but more flexible. multi-user.target is the normal server state, graphical.target adds a desktop, rescue.target is single-user with basic services, emergency.target is a minimal shell, and network-online.target means the network is configured. Units hook in via WantedBy= in [Install]. Change the default with systemctl set-default, and switch at runtime with systemctl isolate.

first_principles.problem: A server needs to boot into a maintenance state without starting applications.

analogy.title: Building modes: open, after-hours, maintenance, lockdown
analogy.story: Each mode switches on a defined set of systems.
analogy.breaks: Building modes are manual; targets are dependency graphs.

code.text:
systemctl get-default                 # multi-user.target
systemctl isolate rescue.target       # stop apps, keep basic system
systemctl list-dependencies multi-user.target | head
# or at boot: add systemd.unit=rescue.target to kernel cmdline

check.q: What's the difference between rescue.target and emergency.target?
check.a: rescue starts basic system services and mounts in single-user mode; emergency gives a minimal shell with almost nothing started.

the-journal-centralized-logging-with-jou.core: journald collects logs from the kernel, early boot, service stdout and stderr, syslog and the native API into an indexed, structured binary journal with metadata (_SYSTEMD_UNIT, _PID, PRIORITY, _BOOT_ID). journalctl queries it: -u unit, -b boot, -p priority, --since and --until, -f follow, -o json, and _PID= field matches. Persist with Storage=persistent (or a /var/log/journal directory), and control size with SystemMaxUse=. Forward to central logging.

first_principles.problem: A service crashed overnight, and the team can't find its logs because stdout went nowhere.

analogy.title: A central flight recorder for every system
analogy.story: Everything said or done is recorded with time and source, searchable later.
analogy.breaks: Recorders are crash-proof; volatile journals vanish on reboot unless persisted.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Crash cause found in the previous boot's log.

code.text:
journalctl -u orders.service -b -1 -p warning --no-pager | tail -30   # previous boot
journalctl -u orders.service --since '02:00' --until '02:30' -o short-precise
journalctl _PID=4123 -o json-pretty | head
journalctl --disk-usage

check.q: How do you view logs for a service from the previous boot?

best-practice-overrides-and-drop-in-file.core: Never edit vendor unit files in /usr/lib/systemd/system, because package updates overwrite them. Instead create drop-ins with systemctl edit unit, which writes /etc/systemd/system/unit.d/override.conf; only the specified settings are merged on top. List-type settings like ExecStart= must first be cleared with an empty assignment. systemctl cat shows the merged result and systemd-delta lists overrides. A full copy in /etc replaces the unit entirely, which is rarely wanted.

first_principles.problem: A team edits nginx.service directly, and the next package upgrade silently reverts their LimitNOFILE change.

analogy.title: Sticky notes on a manual
analogy.story: You add notes that override specific instructions without rewriting the printed manual, which may be reissued.
analogy.breaks: Sticky notes fall off; drop-ins persist until removed.

code.text:
systemctl edit nginx
# [Service]
# LimitNOFILE=65536
# ExecStart=
# ExecStart=/usr/sbin/nginx -g 'daemon off; worker_processes 8;'
systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl restart nginx
systemctl cat nginx | tail -8
systemd-delta --type=extended

check.q: Why must you add an empty 'ExecStart=' line in a drop-in before setting a new one?
check.a: ExecStart is a list setting; without clearing it, the new value is added to the original instead of replacing it.

the-nuclear-option-masking-services.core: systemctl disable removes a unit's enablement symlinks, but it can still start manually or as a dependency. systemctl mask links the unit to /dev/null so it can't start at all, by hand, by dependency or by socket activation, until unmasked. Use it to prevent conflicting services (iptables vs firewalld), stop unwanted auto-starts (packagekit, cloud services on bare metal), or lock out risky services during incidents. Masked units show as 'masked' in status.

first_principles.problem: A disabled service keeps starting because another unit Wants= it.

analogy.title: Removing a phone from speed dial vs disconnecting the line
analogy.story: Disabling removes it from speed dial, but others can still call it; masking cuts the line.
analogy.breaks: Cut lines are visible; masked units look normal until you check status.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Service can't start by any path.

code.text:
systemctl disable --now cups
systemctl start cups          # still works
systemctl mask --now cups
systemctl start cups          # Failed: Unit cups.service is masked.
systemctl is-enabled cups     # masked

check.q: What's the difference between disabling and masking a systemd unit?
check.a: Disable removes auto-start links but allows manual/dependency starts; mask links the unit to /dev/null so it can't be started at all.
